input.add_to_description: Day 10 ~11 AM: Corvin's signed statement names him Aldous Harrow of Harrow Wharf, Saltmarsh (see [[Aldous Harrow]]). The arbiter has ordered a warrant for his cutter and wharf, pending the keep's justice.

entries.text: notebook: updated The Grey Cloak
time: 1 hour later: Day 10, 10:57:12 AM

Out of the story first: yes, there's word. Corvin dictated his statement to the cellar clerk and signed it last evening, and the arbiter has had it since the morning bell. I'll give you what it says in the scene below.

You step onto the wet quay, wring out your cloak and say it plainly. The arbiter listens with her face still, looking from you to the three shrouded shapes in the skiff, and she doesn't interrupt. When you've said the name, "a hooded man called Aldous, who sailed off with a man named Sparrow", something shifts in her eyes. "Inside," she says. "By the fire. Pell, take the dead to the dead-house and tell the surgeon to look them over. Hand-callouses, tattoos, anything."

The hall's counting-room has a fire and a kettle, and someone brings you hot spiced wine. Kit sits stiffly with her back to the wall, steaming. You give the full account, and it takes an hour. The arbiter writes, and when you reach the Gullspit light she puts her pen down for a moment.

Then she slides Corvin's statement across the table. It is four close-written pages in the cellar clerk's round hand, and under it, signed in Corvin's own neat script, the name you wanted. The "H." of his note, and the man in the grey cloak, is Aldous Harrow of Harrow Wharf, on the east quay. He is a salt-wharf owner and shipmaster who owns the Heron's Tithe, and who employs Sparrow and the man you knew as Master Hale. Corvin says he worked for him for years. He says Harrow was once of Elowen's own order, a fellow road-priest turned to trade, and that he wants the lamp-staff and the Gullspit lamp for what they might open. "I do not know what," Corvin adds at the end. "I know only that he has wanted them for sixteen years."

The arbiter taps the page. "Harrow Wharf is a name every merchant on this quay knows, and not one of them says it loudly. I have no proof against him, only a dead man's mouth and a forger's pen. But I can seal his cutter and his wharf for questioning, and I will." She looks at you. "You've also lit the Gullspit beacon in front of the whole town. He'll know exactly where you are."

It is nearly eleven. You have no spell slots, a hearing that has gone well, and a name.

She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

input.add_to_description: Day 10: per Corvin's statement, called 'Aldous' by Elowen and by Corvin; patron of Master Hale and Sparrow; has hunted Elowen's heir for twenty years. Wren has told the arbiter his name and that the three dead hands came from his ship.

entries.text: notebook: updated The Grey Cloak
time: 1 hour later: Day 10, 10:57:12 AM

Out of the story first. Yes, Corvin has signed. The arbiter has the statement in a sealed folder. It names the man he called "H." I'll give you its contents in the scene.

The arbiter's eyes go from the covered shapes to the sodden girl in front of her, then to the white thread of the lamp still burning across the water. She does not ask a second question. "Pell," she says. "Take the dead to the hall's cold room, and keep their purses and any papers for me. Mistress Ashgrove, you will have a fire, and so will your companion." She turns without another word and walks into the Vantry hall, and you follow.

Her counting-room has a fire, a long table, two chairs, and a pot of hot spiced cider that arrives before you've finished sitting. You give her the account in order: the Wick-House, Sparrow in the lane, the Heron's Tithe, the Gullspit light, Brann, the three hands who attacked you, and the Grey Cloak who called himself nothing, whom Brann and Elowen knew as Aldous. She writes it all down in a small, fast hand, and when you reach the lamp she stops writing and looks at you for a moment.

Then she opens a sealed folder and reads you Corvin's statement, in a plain, even voice. Corvin was Elowen Ashgrove's apprentice some twenty-five years ago, a road-priest of the Lantern-Bearer, and he turned to forging and selling blessings. Twenty-one years ago, on the Saltmarsh quay, a hooded patron he knew only as Aldous paid him to find Elowen and, later, her child. The one called "H." is Master Hale, Aldous's hand and factor, whom Corvin first met at Thornhallow. Sparrow is Hale's man, and also answers to Aldous. Corvin swears he never gave Aldous the child's whereabouts, and that he raised you himself, in part to keep you from Aldous, though he admits he used you as well. He says he told Aldous nothing of the coffer, the staff or the lamp until three weeks ago, when Hale's pressure forced him to send for you.

Every word of it is in Corvin's polished style. It could be the truth, or the best-built lie he has ever made. The statement is signed in his hand, witnessed by the cellar guard and the arbiter, and sealed.

"I'll send word to Dame Crowe," the arbiter says. "Master Hale is already in her court's keeping, and I'll ask that he be questioned about this Aldous." She sets the pen down. "Corvin has asked once more to see you. It is your choice. I would not, but I am not you."

It is nearly eleven. You have no spell slots, Kit's hurt arm needs rest, and you have a name, Aldous, to carry to Marrowford at month's end.

input.add_to_description: Day 10 ~11 AM: Wren gave the arbiter her full account by the hall fire. The three dead hands were examined: each wore a small iron heron badge; no names. The arbiter issued warrants for the Heron's Tithe and ordered the east quay watched.

entries.text: notebook: updated Vantry Hall

The arbiter's mouth tightens at the word "Aldous". It isn't a flinch, but you notice it. She doesn't ask you to repeat yourself. She lifts a hand to Pell and the guards, who take the dead from the skiff with a stretcher-cloth apiece. Then she says, "Indoors. By a fire. Before you drip into the quay."

Out of the story first: yes, Corvin has signed. Overnight, before the Vantry clerk and the arbiter, he dictated the whole statement and signed it. It gives Elowen's route, Lantern's Rest, then Ashby Weir, with Saltmarsh by ship afterward, and puts her last alive at Ashby Weir, as he told you. It names the "H." in his note as Master Hale, who he says answers to a hooded patron whose name he never learned. "He called himself only the Patron, and the ship was a grey-sailed cutter." Hale is already held for Dame Crowe, so you could put questions to him at her Marrowford assize at month's end. When the arbiter heard "Aldous" from you, she set that name against nothing she knew. She will have it written into the file.

In the story, you sit by the hall fire with a hot posset in your hands and Kit dripping across from you. You give the arbiter the full account in order, from the Wick-House to the spit. She listens with her eyes half shut, then has your account written out. Each of the three dead hands wore a small iron heron badge on a cord, but no names. She issues warrants for the Heron's Tithe and sets watchers on the east quay. By eleven you are dry, fed, and heavy-limbed.

The arbiter folds her hands. "Mistress Ashgrove, you have saved this town more trouble than you know. The sealing is dead, the Drays are grateful, and my hall owes you. What would you do with the day?"

It's a little past eleven. You're out of spell slots and short of Inspiration, but whole. Your reliquary burns on the spit, the Wick-House is across the quay, and Corvin is in the cellar behind his signature. What does Wren do?

You wring out your cloak, meet the arbiter's eyes, and give it to her in a few plain sentences: the three dead hands, the hooded man called Aldous, Sparrow, the grey sail. She doesn't interrupt. When you finish she looks at the covered shapes in the skiff, then at the white thread of the Gullspit light burning through the rain, and she says, "Indoors, and by a fire. Pell, get these men to the dead-house and find the girl something dry."

An hour later you're sitting in the Vantry elder's counting-room, in a borrowed dry cloak, with a mug of hot cider and Kit steaming quietly in the corner. You give the arbiter the full account, from the Salt Gull to the spit. She listens, her stylus still, and when you finish she opens a ribbon-bound leaf on the table.

"Your answer, on Corvin's statement," she says. "It was signed at the evening bell, in his own hand, before my clerk and the cellar guard. It's long. It names towns and dates, and I'll have a copy sealed for Dame Crowe." She taps one line. "And it names the man he called 'H.' Not Hale. Aldous Hale, the elder brother of the Master Hale you left in Thornhallow's cellar, a shipping-factor of this coast, once a lay brother of your Lantern-Bearer. Owner, he says, of a grey-sailed cutter called the Heron's Tithe."

She turns the leaf toward you. According to Corvin, Aldous Hale funded the three forged pedigrees through his younger brother, to buy up the debts of minor houses once their names were shaken. He wanted Elowen's blessings and her staff to sell by the gross. Elowen refused him on the spit sixteen years ago. Corvin swears he never harmed her. The arbiter's mouth is flat. "I would not call that man an honest witness. But he is a consistent one, and your grey cloak and your Sparrow match the page."

She says she can send a Vantry boat for the Gullspit light's keeper, if you like, and a notice to Dame Crowe at Marrowford, in your name. Sir Corwen has sent word that he'd like to see you, with no anger in it. The squall is still hammering the roof. It is half past ten, and Wren has no spell slots, so a long rest is the thing she's owed.

What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Captured Day 12 ~12:35 AM at the Rushlight House, dropped his hand crossbow and surrendered at 4 HP after Faerie Fire and Kit's crossbow. Hired scout, not Sparrow himself. Says: he was told to follow Wren and count heads and to show a shuttered lamp from the Reedlow jetty at dawn so a boat would know where they were; the boat is the Heron's Tithe's longboat, anchored in a creek mouth two miles down the reeds. He was paid by Sparrow; he never saw the Grey Cloak's face but heard the name 'Aldous'. Held by Kit and Tamsin.

entries.text: notebook: renamed Sparrow's Watcher to Dace Hobb; updated Dace Hobb

Your second insult doesn't land either, but you don't need it to. You drop below the sill, breathe Healing Word over your own ribs (a 5, so you're at 12 of 17, with one slot left), and pop back up in the crack of the shutter. The violet light still clings to him. You call the offer to the whole yard: a bandage and his life if he surrenders, a crossbow bolt in the back if he runs.

The scout looks at the lit yard, the dark byre where Kit's bolt-head glints, the ferry shed where the hook shifts, and the blood running down his sleeve. He lets the hand crossbow fall and raises both hands. "Done," he says hoarsely. "I'm done. Don't loose again."

Kit comes out of the byre in no hurry, shield up and a bolt on the string. Tamsin takes his knife and his belt without a word. He is a lean, tired man called Dace Hobb, with a long scar through one eyebrow. He sits on the water-butt while Kit presses a cloth to his arm, and he talks quickly, as a man does who knows what the alternative is.

Sparrow hired him two days ago in Saltmarsh. His orders were simple: follow the girl with the staff, count who was with her, and show a shuttered lamp from the Reedlow jetty at dawn so a boat would know where to come. The boat is the Heron's Tithe's longboat, hidden in a creek mouth in the reeds about two miles downriver, with four hands and Sparrow aboard. "I never saw the grey one's face," he says. "I heard the name Aldous once, and I'd as soon not have." He looks at the cloth on his arm. "They'll come at dawn if they see no lamp, and they'll come angry if they see one and you aren't what I said."

It is well past midnight. Faerie Fire has gone out, and the fight is over (475 XP now, 100 for the scout). You have 12 of 17 hit points, one 1st-level slot, two Bardic Inspirations, Kit unhurt, Tamsin with her hook, and a prisoner. Annis calls from the dark house that the kettle is on. About four hours of night remain before the dawn lamp. What does Wren do?
